title: Typing API Responses
summary: Treat every API response as unknown, validate it in one typed fetch helper, model the outcomes as a union, and walk paginated APIs with an async generator.
intro: A response from another service is the edge your code crosses most often, and the one you control least: fields get renamed, a proxy answers with HTML, a rate limit kicks in. `fetch` types the body as `any`, so none of that is caught. In this lesson you send every request through one generic helper that validates the body with a zod schema, turn status codes into a union of outcomes that your code has to handle, and read paginated lists page by page. There's no network in this course's sandbox, so every program passes in a fake `fetch` that returns real `Response` objects, which is also how you test code like this.

steps.title: A typed fetch helper

examples.title: The any in res.json()
examples.prompt: Fetch a user from a fake API whose response renamed `email` to `mail`, and return the body as a `User` without checking it.
examples.errorIncludes: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toLowerCase')
examples.explanation: `body` is `any`, as the bubble shows, so `return body` passes as a `User` with no check at all, and `getUser`'s return type makes a promise the code can't keep. The name prints, then `user.email` is `undefined`, and the program crashes on a line that looks perfectly typed. In a real app that line can be far away from the request, which makes the bug hard to trace. The fix is to treat the body as `unknown` and validate it where it arrives, as the next example does.

examples.title: getJson
examples.prompt: Write `getJson`, which checks the status and validates the body with a schema, and fetch three products: one that's valid, one with a wrong field, and one that doesn't exist.
examples.output:
MUG-001: Mug, 1250 cents
TEA-002: bad response: priceCents: Invalid input: expected number, received string
PLT-404: HTTP 404
examples.explanation: `getJson` is generic in the schema. `S` is inferred from the schema you pass, so with `Product` the result has the product's type, as the bubble shows, and nothing is annotated at the call. Inside, the body is `unknown`, so the only way to use it is through `schema.parse`. A status outside 200 to 299 throws an `HttpError` that carries the status, and a body that doesn't fit throws a `ZodError` that names the field. Either way the bad data stops at the edge, and the caller tells the two failures apart with `instanceof`. Any other error is rethrown, because this loop doesn't know how to handle it.

examples.title: Injecting fetch
examples.prompt: Give `getJson` the real `fetch` as a default, and pass a fake that answers from a table of routes and records every request.
examples.explanation: `fetchFn: typeof fetch = fetch` gives the parameter the exact type of the real `fetch`, and the real `fetch` as its default. In production you call `getJson(url, Weather)`, and the request goes to the network. Examples and tests pass a fake instead, and anything that fits `typeof fetch` will do: an async function that takes the URL and resolves to a `Response`. Because `fakeApi` answers with real `Response` objects, `getJson` runs exactly the code it runs in production, status check and all. The fake also records each path it was asked for, so a test can check which requests were made. There's no network to wait for, and every run prints the same thing.

practice.title: Get a user
practice.prompt:
Fetch three users through `getJson`, and print one line for each outcome. The starter has `HttpError`, `getJson`, and a fake API that knows users 1 and 2.

1. Make the `User` schema check that `id` is a whole number, `name` has at least 1 character, and `email` is an email address.
2. Make `getUser(id, fetchFn)` get `https://api.example.com/users/<id>` with `getJson` and `User`.
3. For an `HttpError`, print `user <id>: HTTP <status>`.
4. For a `ZodError`, print `user <id>: bad response: <path>: <message>` for each issue.

Expected output:

```text
user 1: Grace Hopper <grace@example.com>
user 2: bad response: email: Invalid email address
user 3: HTTP 404
```

tests.output:
user 1: Grace Hopper <grace@example.com>
user 2: bad response: email: Invalid email address
user 3: HTTP 404

hints: `getUser` is one line: return the result of `getJson` with the URL, `User`, and `fetchFn`.
`z.email()` is the email schema, and `.int()` and `.min(1)` add the other rules.
In `catch`, check `err instanceof HttpError` first, then `err instanceof z.ZodError`, and loop over `err.issues`, joining each `path` with dots. Rethrow anything else.

steps.title: Responses as a union

examples.title: ApiResult
examples.prompt: Turn four responses into `ApiResult` values: a user, a 404, a 429 with a `Retry-After` header, and a 503.
examples.explanation: Each status becomes the member that carries what a caller needs: the data, nothing more, how long to wait, or the status. `retryAfter` reads the header, which is a string or `null`, and falls back to 60 seconds when it's missing or isn't a number, since servers may also send a date there. The result is an `ApiResult` of the schema's output, as the bubble shows, so the data is only typed inside the `ok` member, and a caller has to check `kind` before touching it. A 400 would throw, because it means this code built a bad request.

examples.title: Error envelopes
examples.prompt: Read the error message out of three failed responses: two in the API's `{ error: { code, message } }` envelope, and one HTML page from a proxy.
examples.output:
404 user_not_found: No user has id 42
409 email_taken: That email is already registered
502 HTTP 502 with no error details
examples.explanation: Many APIs wrap every error in the same envelope, and its message is worth showing to the user. But an error body is still data from outside. A proxy or a load balancer in front of the API can answer with HTML, and `res.json()` throws a `SyntaxError` on that. So `errorMessage` turns a body that isn't JSON into `null` with `.catch(() => null)`, and checks the shape with `safeParse`, which never throws. Every response gets a message, and the HTML page falls back to its status.

examples.title: Exhaustive handling
examples.prompt: Turn each `ApiResult` into a message for the user, with a `switch` that can't miss a kind.
examples.output:
Welcome back, Ada!
We couldn't find that account.
Too many requests. Try again in 2 min.
Something went wrong on our side (503). Please try again.
examples.explanation: Inside each `case`, `result` is narrowed to that member, so `result.data` exists only under `"ok"` and `result.retryAfterSeconds` only under `"rate_limited"`. In `default`, `result` has to be `never`, because every kind is handled. If someone adds a kind to `ApiResult`, say `{ kind: "unauthorized" }`, the call to `assertNever` stops compiling until `message` handles it, so a new outcome can't reach a user as a blank screen. The messages are written for people: minutes rounded up instead of raw seconds, and no JSON.

practice.title: Fetch with outcomes
practice.prompt:
An exchange rate API answers with a rate, a 404, a 429, or a 503. Turn each response into an `ApiResult`, and print what happened.

1. Add two members to `ApiResult`: `{ kind: "rate_limited"; retryAfterSeconds: number }` and `{ kind: "server_error"; status: number }`.
2. In `toApiResult`, a status from 200 to 299 is `ok`, with the body parsed by `schema`. 404 is `not_found`.
3. 429 is `rate_limited`, with the seconds from the `Retry-After` header, or 60 when it's missing or not a number.
4. 500 and above is `server_error`, and any other status throws an `Error`.
5. Add the two new cases to `describe`: `rate limited, retry in <n> s` and `server error <status>`.
6. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `ApiResult` from your file.

Expected output:

```text
EUR: 0.92
not found
rate limited, retry in 30 s
server error 503
```

tests.output:
EUR: 0.92
not found
rate limited, retry in 30 s
server error 503

cases.name: a rate limit must say how long to wait

hints: Add the members with `|`, the way the first example writes its union. Then the `switch` in `describe` stops compiling until it has a case for each new kind.
Check the statuses in order: `res.ok` first, then 404, then 429, then `res.status >= 500`, and throw for anything left.
`Number.parseInt(res.headers.get("Retry-After") ?? "", 10)` is `NaN` when the header is missing, so check it with `Number.isNaN` and use 60 instead.

steps.title: Generic page schemas

examples.title: pageOf
examples.prompt: Write `pageOf` once, and build page schemas for products and for orders from it.
examples.output:
Mug, Tea, next: p2
1 order, last page: true
examples.explanation: `pageOf` takes a schema and returns a new one around it. Its return type isn't written out: TypeScript infers it from the `z.object` the function builds, so it still knows which item schema went in. That's why `ProductPage` parses to products and `OrderPage` to orders, as the bubbles show, from one function. `nextCursor` is `.nullable()` because the last page has no next page, and the orders page says so with `null`.

examples.title: Walking pages
examples.prompt: Read every product from a fake API with three pages, with an async generator that follows `nextCursor`.
examples.output:
MUG-001 Mug
TEA-002 Tea
PLT-003 Plate
CUP-004 Cup
JAR-005 Jar
pages fetched: first, c2, c3
examples.explanation: The generator fetches a page, checks it with `ProductPage`, yields its items one at a time, and then follows `nextCursor` until it's `null`. Every item has been checked before it leaves the generator, so the loop only ever sees valid products, typed as `Product`. The caller writes a plain `for await` and never sees a cursor or a URL. The last line shows the fake was asked for each page once, in order. Pages are fetched only as the loop asks for more items, so a loop that stops early with `break` never fetches the pages after it.

examples.title: A bad item on page 2
examples.prompt: Walk the same kind of pages when page 2 has a product without a name, and report the page and the field.
examples.output:
MUG-001 Mug
TEA-002 Tea
page 2 is invalid:
✖ Invalid input: expected string, received undefined
  → at items[1].name
examples.explanation: Page 1 is fine, so its products print. Page 2's second item has no `name`. The whole page is checked before any of it is yielded, so `Plate` never prints either: a page is accepted or rejected as a unit. The error says which page failed, and `z.prettifyError` adds the path inside it, `items[1].name`, the second item's name. The `catch` around the `for await` gets the error like any other error thrown in the loop. That's enough to find the bad record in the API's data, where a bare `TypeError` three functions later would not be.

practice.title: All customers
practice.prompt:
Read every customer from a paginated API. The starter has the `Customer` schema and a fake API with three pages.

1. Make `pageOf(item)` return a schema for a page: `items`, an array of `item`, and `nextCursor`, a string or `null`.
2. Make `allCustomers(fetchFn)` start at `https://api.example.com/customers`, then fetch `https://api.example.com/customers?cursor=<nextCursor>` until `nextCursor` is `null`.
3. Check each page with `pageOf(Customer)`, and yield every customer.
4. Collect the customers with `Array.fromAsync(allCustomers(fakeFetch))`, so the starter prints each name and the count.
5. Keep `export`: hidden type tests import `allCustomers` and `Customer` from your file.

Expected output:

```text
Ada Lovelace
Grace Hopper
Alan Turing
Katherine Johnson
Edsger Dijkstra
5 customers
```

tests.output:
Ada Lovelace
Grace Hopper
Alan Turing
Katherine Johnson
Edsger Dijkstra
5 customers

hints: `pageOf` is the function from the examples: `z.object` with `items: z.array(item)` and `nextCursor: z.string().nullable()`.
Keep the next URL in `let url: string | null` and loop `while (url !== null)`. After yielding a page's items, set `url` from `nextCursor`, or to `null` on the last page.
`Array.fromAsync` takes the generator and resolves to an array of everything it yields: `const customers = await Array.fromAsync(allCustomers(fakeFetch))`.

recap:
- `await res.json()` is `any`. Store the body as `unknown` and validate it with a schema before anything reads it.
- `getJson<S extends z.ZodType>(url, schema, fetchFn = fetch): Promise<z.output<S>>` checks the status, parses the body, and returns the schema's output type.
- Take `fetch` as a parameter typed `typeof fetch`. Production uses the real one, and tests pass a fake that answers with `Response.json(...)`.
- Model the outcomes callers should handle as a union (`ok`, `not_found`, `rate_limited`, `server_error`), switch on `kind` exhaustively, and throw for statuses that mean a bug.
- Error bodies come from outside too: parse their envelope with `safeParse`, and survive a body that isn't JSON.
- `pageOf(item)` builds a page schema for any item schema, and an async generator walks the pages, checking each one before it yields the items.
